claims.claim: A color wheel is a tool that shows the relationships among primary, secondary, and tertiary colors, arranging hues in a circle; Isaac Newton was the first to bend the spectrum into such a circular arrangement.

On the traditional artists' wheel the primaries are red, yellow, and blue (RYB); secondary colors (orange, green, violet) are made by mixing two primaries; and tertiary colors are made by mixing a primary with a neighboring secondary, yielding a twelve-hue wheel. Systems based on light or on printing inks use different primaries, which is why the RYB wheel is a convention for pigment mixing rather than a law of physics.

Any color can be described by three properties: hue (the pure state of a color, its identity and position on the wheel, set by wavelength), saturation (also called chroma or intensity, the degree of a hue's concentration from vivid to dull), and value (the lightness or darkness of the color).

Value and saturation are independent: a hue can be made lighter or darker (value) without becoming more or less vivid (saturation), and saturation can be lowered by adding white, black, gray, or the complementary color.
Adding white to a hue makes a tint, adding black makes a shade, and adding gray makes a tone; all three change value and/or saturation without changing the underlying hue.

Colors are grouped as warm (reds, oranges, yellows) or cool (greens, blues, violets) relative to one another; the strongest temperature polarity is between red-orange and blue-green, and warm colors conventionally appear to advance while cool colors appear to recede.
Complementary colors sit opposite each other on the wheel and give the strongest possible hue contrast; when two complements are mixed they neutralize each other toward a gray or neutral.

Standard color harmonies are defined by position on the wheel: monochromatic (one hue in varied value and saturation), analogous (neighboring hues), complementary (opposite hues), split-complementary (a hue plus the two neighbors of its complement), triadic (three hues evenly spaced 120 degrees apart), and tetradic (two complementary pairs, forming a rectangle or square).

A color's appearance depends on the colors around it: two adjacent colors influence each other and change our perception of them, a phenomenon called simultaneous contrast, first described by the chemist Michel-Eugene Chevreul in 1839 and demonstrated at length in Josef Albers's 1963 book Interaction of Color, which opens with the idea that color is the most relative medium in art.

Color 'meanings' are a learned response and a cultural convention rather than an established science: some associations cross cultural boundaries but symbolism often varies across time and place (for example, red signals danger on a stop sign but represents good luck in Chinese culture).

Empirical cross-cultural research finds a mixed picture: some color-valence and color-emotion associations recur across cultures while others differ significantly between cultural groups, so blanket claims that a given color universally causes a given feeling are not supported.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether color-emotion associations are universal or culturally specific.
positions: Popular 'color psychology' asserts fixed, universal meanings (red = passion, blue = calm, etc.).

Peer-reviewed cross-cultural work (Kawai et al. 2022) finds both shared and culture-specific patterns depending on the color pairing and the cultural group, and design OER frames color symbolism as a learned response that varies across time and place.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents color associations as useful design conventions and learned cultural associations, explicitly notes that they vary across cultures and are not settled science, and cites both the OER caution and the peer-reviewed finding rather than asserting universal meanings.

positions: The artists' pigment wheel treats red, yellow, and blue as primaries.
Color made from light and color made from printing inks use different primary sets.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the RYB wheel as the traditional artists' convention, states plainly that light and print use different primaries, and defers the additive/subtractive mechanics to the color-models sibling topic to avoid duplication.

Read section pages on 2026-08-19: Color Systems (color wheel shows relationships among primary/secondary/tertiary colors; Newton first arranged the spectrum in a circle); Understanding Hue (hue = the pure state of a color, determined by wavelength; primaries red/yellow/blue as the extreme of hue contrast); Understanding Value (value = lightness or darkness of hue; value read before hue); Understanding Saturation ('chromatic intensity; the degree of concentration or suffusion of a hue from vivid to dull'; saturation reduced by adding white, black, gray, or the complement); Understanding Temperature (warm vs cool grouping; strongest polarity between red-orange and blue-green); Understanding Complementary Contrast (complements opposite on the wheel, strongest hue contrast, neutralize to a neutral when mixed); Understanding Simultaneous Contrast (two adjacent colors influence each other; Chevreul 1839; Albers, Interaction of Color, 1963, 'color is the most relative medium in art'); Understanding Color Symbolism (color meaning is a learned response that varies across time and place; red = danger on a stop sign but good luck in Chinese culture). The book is a mixed-license LibreTexts collection, so treated as REFERENCE_ONLY; facts synthesized, no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The good, the bad, and the red: implicit color-valence associations across cultures
sourceRecords.provider: Psychological Research (Kawai, Zhang, Lukacs, Chu, Zheng, Gao, Gozli, Wang, Ansorge)
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed study (Psychological Research, 2022), read via PMC on 2026-08-19. Finds that implicit color-valence associations show both shared and culture-specific patterns: red-positivity associations appeared even in the Austrian sample within the red-white system, while the Western group showed a significantly stronger color-valence interaction than the Mainland Chinese group for the red-green opposition. Used to support the claim that color-emotion associations are empirically mixed (partly shared, partly cultural), not a settled universal science. REFERENCE_ONLY; facts summarized, no text reproduced.
